news.title: Oil prices fall as supply concerns linger after Iran claims mine strikes on ships, World News - AsiaOne.com
news.summary:
LONDON - Crude oil prices fell on Thursday (Nov 26) following the previous session's sharp rise, as supply concerns lingered after Yemen's Houthis said they hit ​Saudi Arabia's largest oil refinery and Iran said mines struck ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude futures were down 82 cents, or 0.87 per cent, at US$93.79 (S$121) a barrel at 0939 GMT (5.39pm SGT). US West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 35 cents, or 0.42 per cent, to $83.33 a barrel.

There will be no settlement for WTI on Thursday because of the US Thanksgiving holiday.

"The perceived supply surplus in the coming months and quarters and sticky inflation, which forces central banks to raise rates, resulting in a stronger dollar, will possibly set a ceiling on any attempt to push prices significantly higher," said PVM Oil Associates analyst Tamas Varga.

"The new trading range, it appears, is around $88-$97, basis Brent."

Brent settled up 3.5 per cent in the previous session, while WTI climbed 2 per cent after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said they had attacked ​Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery ‌and Riyadh's financial district.

The refinery, Saudi ​Arabia's largest, is part ​of a complex that also serves as a major export terminal for Saudi crude, and analysts expect the latest reported Houthi attacks to increase oil's geopolitical risk premium. The Saudi government and state oil firm Aramco did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

At the same time, shipping has been disrupted through the key Strait of Hormuz, where oil supply had been recovering to near pre-war levels.

An oil tanker hit a naval mine and caught fire in a "restricted zone" in the strait on Wednesday, the semi-official Fars news agency cited the Iranian Army as saying in a statement.

That report came after state media said two oil tankers struck mines and exploded in the strait on Wednesday.

"The broadening of the Middle East conflict threatens to halt the recovery in oil flows in recent weeks," said ANZ analyst Daniel Hynes. "Persian Gulf crude exports rose last week but remain on a declining trend."

OPEC+ ministers will hold meetings on Nov 29 to decide their 2027 output policy.

They face the challenge of balancing output with the United Arab Emirates no longer in the group, and with Iraq and Kazakhstan pressing OPEC+ to raise its estimate of their oil production capacity.

In the US, crude stocks rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended Nov 20, the Energy Information Administration said, also supporting prices as analysts had expected a 1.5-million-barrel rise.

In Asia, Thailand's Bangchak Corp said it had shut all production units at its Phra Khanong oil refinery in Bangkok following a fire.

news.title: US Inflation Hits 3.8%: Will the Fed Raise Interest Rates Again in December? - TradingView
news.summary:
US inflation is putting fresh pressure on financial markets as October’s latest Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) report shows price growth accelerating faster than the Federal Reserve would prefer. Headline PCE inflation reached 3.8% annually, while core inflation climbed to 3.3%, its highest level in nearly three years. The data complicates the Fed’s December policy decision, particularly as economic growth remains resilient.

With investors already reassessing technology valuations and interest-rate expectations, the latest inflation figures raise a bigger question: could the Federal Reserve deliver another rate hike before the end of 2026?

Core PCE Inflation Raises the Biggest Concern

The latest report shows that inflationary pressure is becoming more persistent rather than fading toward the Fed’s 2% objective. While the monthly headline increase moderated, core PCE accelerated annually, suggesting underlying price pressures remain difficult to contain.

The Federal Reserve closely monitors PCE inflation when assessing progress toward its 2% target. The latest core reading therefore gives policymakers another reason to remain cautious about easing monetary policy.

Strong US GDP Growth Complicates the Fed’s Decision

Inflation is not the only challenge facing policymakers. The U.S. economy expanded at an annualized rate of 4.3% in the third quarter, significantly above the earlier estimate of 3.4%. Consumer spending and business investment contributed to the upward revision. Consumer spending increased 0.3% in October, while stronger investment in equipment and technology continued to support economic activity.

🚨BREAKING: US inflation rises to 3.8%, but underlying inflation comes in lower than expected at 3.1%!

Meanwhile, fewer Americans are claiming unemployment benefits than expected, and personal incomes are rising faster than forecast.

Inflation remains stubborn, but the US… pic.twitter.com/HufXIwCUCo

This combination of resilient growth and elevated inflation gives the Fed less reason to rush toward interest-rate cuts. At the same time, policymakers must consider whether additional tightening could weaken economic activity or intensify pressure on businesses and households.

December Fed Rate Decision: Another Hike Is on the Table

The Federal Reserve’s December 8–9 meeting is becoming increasingly important for investors. The central bank currently maintains its federal funds target range at 3.75%–4.00%. Following the latest inflation report, financial markets have priced in a strong probability of a 25-basis-point increase, potentially taking the range to 4.00%–4.25%.

UPDATE: 🇺🇸 Market expectations for the December Fed decision:

-> 97.8% expect a 25 bps rate hike

-> 2.2% expect no hike pic.twitter.com/SoZGBjxg37

However, policymakers remain divided over the appropriate response. Fed Governor Christopher Waller has indicated that a larger increase could be considered, while other officials have advocated a more measured approach. The decision will also include updated economic projections, offering investors a clearer indication of how policymakers view inflation and interest rates heading into 2027.

Why Rising Inflation Matters for Nasdaq and AI Stocks

The inflation outlook has direct implications for U.S. equities, particularly high-growth technology and AI stocks. Higher interest rates increase the discount rate applied to future corporate earnings, potentially putting pressure on valuations. Companies whose share prices depend heavily on expectations of future growth can become particularly vulnerable when Treasury yields and borrowing costs rise.

That creates another challenge for Nvidia, AMD, Micron and other semiconductor companies already facing questions over AI valuations and infrastructure spending.

If the Fed signals further tightening, technology stocks could face renewed valuation pressure. Conversely, a more cautious policy outlook could provide relief to growth shares, although persistent inflation would remain a concern.

What Comes Next for the US Stock Market?

The December Fed meeting is now the central event for investors assessing the direction of U.S. equities, bond yields and the dollar. The combination of 3.8% inflation and 4.3% economic growth makes an immediate shift toward monetary easing increasingly difficult to justify.

For Wall Street, the risk is that higher borrowing costs could collide with already elevated technology valuations. The next Fed decision could determine whether the recent pressure on Nasdaq stocks deepens or whether investors find room for another recovery heading into 2027.

news.title: Gold drifts lower as Fed rate-hike fears loom - Kitco
news.summary:
Nov 26 (Reuters) - Gold prices drifted lower on Thursday, as lingering ​inflation concerns and the market's growing expectations that the US Federal Reserve will ‌hike interest rates again pressured the precious metal.

Spot gold was down 0.5% to $3,564.06 per ounce by 1111 GMT. Prices briefly fell below the psychologically key $3,500 level on Wednesday for the first time since September ​2025. US gold futures for December delivery rose 0.8% to $3,562.60. "Spot gold is testing support ​around the mid-$3,000 region. Gold is unlikely to see a sustained rebound ⁠until markets sense that the Fed is nearing the end of its rate-hike cycle," ​said Han Tan, chief market analyst at Bybit.

"Bullion bulls are set to be kept on ​the back foot... But fresh risk-off events across global financial markets may support the precious metal, adding to persistent purchases from central banks." Robust domestic demand is fuelling inflation in the US, with a measure of ​underlying price pressures in October posting its biggest year-over-year increase since late 2023, data ​showed on Wednesday. It reinforced expectations that the Fed will raise interest rates next month and again ‌in ⁠early 2027. The Fed's last rate hike, the first in three years, was delivered in September.

While gold is traditionally viewed as an inflation hedge, elevated rates can weigh on the non-yielding asset.

Given that risks exist, "it is likely too early to call a bottom in gold, ​and indeed in the ​precious metals complex," ⁠analysts at TD Securities said in a note.

"Long-term, however, the yellow metal along with the precious metals complex should see significant upside. ​Indeed, gold prices will likely start trending towards $5,000/oz in the latter ​part of ⁠next year, as investors muse about easing policy rates."

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump fired a new tariff salvo on Wednesday on goods from 14 major trading partners including China, Japan and the ⁠European Union.

Among ​other metals, spot silver rose 0.6% to $41.474 per ​ounce, platinum gained 1.3% to $1,295.31 and palladium climbed 1.6% to $875.45 per ounce.

US markets were closed on Thursday for the ​Thanksgiving holiday.

Reporting by Ashitha Shivaprasad in Bengaluru; Editing by Harikrishnan Nair and Joe Bavier

news.title: Why Gasoline Prices Are Falling While Diesel Remains Expensive - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
news.summary: Americans heading into the Thanksgiving holiday are finally getting some relief at the gasoline pump. After months of elevated prices, the national average has fallen sharply in November, dropping to approximately $3.66 per gallon as of November 21. That's a welcome development for millions of holiday travelers, although gasoline remains considerably more expensive than it was a year ago. Diesel prices have also declined recently, but they remain much higher than gasoline. According to the Energy Information Administration EIA, diesel averaged $5.94 per gallon during the week of November 16, compared with $3.81 for regular gasoline. As I explained in October, the enormous gap between gasoline and diesel prices reflects changes in fuel specifications, global demand, refinery economics, and increasingly tight distillate supplies. The huge divergence has created an unusual situation for America's oil refineries. While consumers are celebrating cheaper gasoline, refiners have been operating at exceptionally high rates to take advantage of strong diesel margins. They have also been making significant adjustments to the products they manufacture from crude oil, shifting production away from gasoline and toward diesel and jet fuel. But if refiners are deliberately reducing gasoline yields, why are gasoline prices falling so rapidly The answer illustrates how refinery economics, crude oil prices, and seasonal demand interact in ways that aren't always obvious to consumers. Refineries Can't Simply Choose What to Produce One of the important things to understand about petroleum refining is that gasoline and diesel are not produced independently. When a refinery processes crude oil, it produces a mixture of products, including gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, liquefied petroleum gases, and other materials. The proportions depend on the crude oil being processed, the refinery's equipment, and the operating conditions. As I've explained in an earlier analysis of America's diesel shortage, having ample crude oil doesn't necessarily mean having enough refining capacity configured to produce the petroleum products consumers need. Refineries have considerable flexibility, but they cannot simply convert every barrel of crude oil into diesel, regardless of how profitable it becomes. Historically, U.S. refineries have produced approximately 45 to 50 barrels of gasoline for every 100 barrels of crude oil processed. But an EIA analysis published November 5 revealed that gasoline yields averaged less than 45% from January through August 2026. In fact, gasoline yields were below the previous five-year low in every one of those months. At the same time, distillate yields were above their five-year average, and jet fuel yields reached historically elevated levels. Beginning in March, jet fuel yields reached at least 12% and remained at or above that level through August. These changes were not accidental. Refiners were responding to the greater profitability of producing middle distillates, particularly diesel and jet fuel, as global supplies remained constrained. High Diesel Margins Are Keeping Refineries Busy The financial incentive behind these operating decisions is straightforward. Refiners earn money on the difference between what they pay for crude oil and what they receive for the products they sell, after accounting for operating and other costs. One common measure of that opportunity is the crack spread, which compares the market price of a refined product with the cost of crude oil. When diesel crack spreads are substantially higher than gasoline crack spreads, refiners have a strong incentive to maximize diesel production. That doesn't mean gasoline becomes unprofitable, but it does change the relative attractiveness of the products. Refinery operators respond by adjusting their operations to capture as much of the higher-value product as their equipment will allow. The result has been exceptionally high refinery utilization. According to an October 22 EIA report, U.S. refinery utilization averaged more than 95% of capacity between May and September, the highest for those months since 1998. The EIA specifically identified tight global supplies and strong diesel margins as major incentives for those elevated operating rates. That doesn't mean refineries are producing record volumes of petroleum products. U.S. refining capacity has declined since 2019, so even exceptionally high utilization rates don't necessarily translate into record output. But this creates an interesting distinction between gasoline yields and gasoline production. A refinery can reduce the percentage of each barrel of crude devoted to gasoline while still maintaining substantial gasoline output if it increases the total volume of crude processed. Consider a simplified example. Suppose a refinery processes 100,000 barrels of crude per day with a gasoline yield of 48%. That would produce approximately 48,000 barrels of gasoline daily. If the refinery increases crude throughput to 110,000 barrels per day but reduces its gasoline yield to 44%, gasoline production would actually increase slightly to 48,400 barrels per day. The refinery is producing a smaller percentage of gasoline, but more gasoline in absolute terms. Actual refinery operations are more complicated because of processing gains, blending components, and ethanol additions, but the illustration captures an important principle. This doesn't establish that refiners chasing diesel profits are responsible for the recent decline in gasoline prices. It does explain how strong diesel economics can help sustain gasoline supplies, even as refiners deliberately shift their product yields away from gasoline. What's Actually Driving Gasoline Prices Lower The most direct explanation for the recent gasoline price decline is falling crude oil prices. According to AAA, crude oil had retreated into the low $80-per-barrel range by November 19, helping pull gasoline prices lower. Because crude oil represents the largest underlying cost of producing gasoline, declining crude prices generally translate into lower retail prices, although the relationship isn't instantaneous. Seasonal demand is another important factor. As I've explained previously, gasoline prices typically decline in the fall as summer driving demand subsides and refiners transition to less expensive winter gasoline blends. Summer gasoline specifications restrict volatility to reduce evaporative emissions, while the return to winter specifications allows refiners to blend more inexpensive butane into gasoline. That increases available gasoline supplies while reducing production costs. Inventories provide additional evidence that gasoline supplies are relatively comfortable. For the week ending November 13, EIA reported that U.S. gasoline inventories increased by 5.2 million barrels to 215.9 million barrels. That placed gasoline inventories approximately 3% above their five-year seasonal average. Distillate inventories told a very different story. Although they increased by 1.6 million barrels during the same week, total distillate stocks stood at just 104.9 million barrels, approximately 7% below their five-year average. That difference helps explain why diesel continues to command such a substantial premium over gasoline. It is important not to draw too much from a single weekly inventory report. Gasoline inventories reflect domestic production, imports, exports, and consumption, and movements in any of these categories can influence the weekly balance. Nevertheless, the contrast between relatively comfortable gasoline supplies and tight distillate inventories is consistent with the price divergence consumers are seeing. The important conclusion is that falling gasoline prices are being driven by several factors working together. Lower crude oil prices and seasonal demand weakness are major contributors, while elevated refinery operating rates may be helping maintain gasoline supplies despite refiners' efforts to favor diesel production. Cheaper Gasoline Doesn't Mean the Energy Crisis Is Over The decline in gasoline prices is welcome news for motorists, but the continuing diesel premium presents a different economic challenge. Heavy-duty trucks, agricultural machinery, construction equipment, and freight transportation all depend heavily on diesel fuel. When diesel prices remain elevated, those costs can eventually work their way into the prices consumers pay for food, building materials, and other products. This helps explain why falling gasoline prices don't necessarily translate into an equally large reduction in the cost of living. Consumers may save money filling their personal vehicles while businesses continue paying elevated transportation and distribution costs. The economic impact of diesel extends well beyond the relatively small number of Americans who own diesel-powered passenger vehicles. It also illustrates why the gasoline and diesel markets cannot be viewed entirely separately. Both products emerge from the same refining system, and refiners continually adjust their operations in response to changing prices and demand. Strong diesel margins can encourage higher refinery throughput, potentially supporting gasoline supplies, even when refiners are deliberately reducing gasoline's share of their output. The Bottom Line The recent decline in gasoline prices is good news for consumers, but it doesn't mean the pressures that drove fuel prices higher throughout 2026 have disappeared. Diesel supplies remain relatively tight, and refiners continue to face strong economic incentives to prioritize middle-distillate production. The surprising development is that refiners have been reducing gasoline yields while maintaining unusually high operating rates. These are not contradictory trends. They reflect an industry responding to changing market conditions within the physical limitations of its equipment. The biggest drivers of cheaper gasoline remain falling crude prices, seasonal demand, and relatively comfortable gasoline inventories. But strong diesel margins have created an additional incentive for refiners to operate at high rates, potentially helping sustain gasoline supplies even as they shift their product yields toward diesel and jet fuel. For Thanksgiving travelers, that combination has helped create some welcome relief at the pump. For the broader economy, however, the persistent diesel premium is a reminder that cheaper gasoline doesn't necessarily mean lower transportation costs across the board. By Robert Rapier

news.title: Trump admin.: New tariffs on 14 countries, including China and Japan - Denver Gazette
news.summary:
The Trump administration put forth a new plan to impose tariffs on imports from 14 U.S. trade partners, including China , the European Union, Japan, and Taiwan, escalating a global trade war.

Chinese imports will face a 20% levy, but it could rise to 40% if a trade truce between the United States and China doesn’t yield a favorable deal. The truce would have expired this month, but it will be extended to January.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer announced the proposal on Wednesday under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. He accused the 14 nations of imposing unreasonable, burdensome restrictions on U.S. commerce after an eight-month investigation. Those nations include China, the 27-member European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.

“For decades, many of our trading partners have adopted industrial strategies built on targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression, financial and other support, non-market economy inputs, and other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America’s manufacturing base,” Greer said.

Greer also claimed the levies would “level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.”

Levies on trade partners will not exceed those agreed upon in previously agreed-upon bilateral trade frameworks. The EU previously agreed to a 15% cap on tariffs, as did Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan.

The administration has also not imposed tariffs on Mexico or Norway at this time.

Before Wednesday’s announcement, the administration had finalized a 10% or 12.5% tariff imposed in July on 60 trading partners, citing Section 301. The new tariffs won’t stack on top of the tariffs finalized in July, excluding China.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun slammed the new levies at a press conference. “The so-called “overcapacity” is a false proposition, and China opposes using it as a pretext for political manipulation,” Guo said.

The administration has relied on Section 301 since the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act in February. Tariff fallout that raised the cost of living helped Democrats flip both chambers of Congress this month. Democrats in the new Congress will likely take aim at the administration over tariffs.

The tariff proposal must first go through a public notice-and-comment period.

news.title: Meeting of 28-29 October 2026 - ECB - Zprávy Kurzy.cz
news.summary:
26 November 2026

Ms Schnabel started her presentation on the latest financial market developments with the observation that higher energy prices since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting on 9-10 September 2026 had reinforced concerns about persistent inflationary pressures. At the same time, market attention had shifted towards fiscal dynamics and concerns about the increasingly debt-financed artificial intelligence ( AI ) investment cycle.

Energy price pressures had intensified substantially since the September meeting, pushing oil and gas prices above the adverse scenario of the September 2026 ECB staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area. In response to renewed tensions in the Middle East, the latest oil futures curve had shifted markedly higher compared with the baseline of the September projections and had also moved visibly above the adverse scenario over the short term. The repricing in gas markets had been even more pronounced, with the futures curve currently standing well above the adverse scenario over the entire horizon.

Diesel refining margins stood at a historically high level, with euro area diesel crack spreads – the differences between wholesale prices and crude oil prices – above the levels observed after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 . Freight rates from the Gulf region to Europe had surged to record highs, while the probability of a US-Iran peace deal by the end of 2026 was at its lowest since the start of the war in the Middle East. The increase in energy prices was reflected in inflation compensation. Inflation fixings throughout 2026 and 2027 had shifted higher, peaking at 4.5% for January 2027 and remaining above 2.5% until the first quarter of 2028 , while inflation fixings for 2028 were broadly unchanged. Option-implied inflation risks continued to be skewed to the upside over the next two years and five years.

Despite the sharp increase in energy prices and the deterioration in the inflation outlook, expectations for the key ECB interest rates stood near their September levels. The one-year overnight index swap (OIS) rate one year ahead had decoupled from energy prices, consistent with communication that interest rates would not move in lockstep with energy costs. Immediately after the Governing Council’s September monetary policy meeting, the OIS forward curve had shifted markedly higher, temporarily pricing in more than four additional 25 basis point hikes over the next 12 months, before investors pared back expectations to just under three additional hikes. Market pricing adjusted for term premia pointed to an expected peak in the deposit facility rate at around 3%, implying a more pronounced tightening than the median expectation of participants in the Survey of Monetary Analysts, which foresaw only one more hike.

Euro area risk-free rates had stabilised and, at longer tenors, had even declined since the September meeting, while US rates had risen across maturities on the back of higher real rates. The divergence between real yields in the euro area and the United States was consistent with investors’ perceptions of a more dynamic US economy.

The rise in euro area ten-year rates relative to the average in 2024 had been driven primarily by higher real term premia, reflecting increased uncertainty about the long - run macroeconomic outlook and a growing net supply of public and private debt. Higher expected short -term real rates and higher inflation expectations accounted for around one-third of the increase in ten-year rates. Moreover, the shift in stock - bond correlations into positive territory pointed to reduced diversification benefits from bonds amid more frequent adverse supply shocks, requiring greater compensation to hold duration risk.

As higher real rates raised governments’ borrowing costs and reduced fiscal space, sovereign bond yields had become more sensitive to differences in the fiscal outlook. Sovereign bond spreads had increased notably for some countries since the previous monetary policy meeting, but they had generally remained well below earlier peaks and broadly in line with fundamentals. A greater responsiveness of euro area sovereign bond yields to market stress also reflected a shift towards more price-sensitive investors. Despite the recent widening in spreads, systemic stress indicators had remained contained, well below levels recorded in previous episodes of market strain.

Euro area bank equities had overall remained resilient and, despite a recent correction, had continued to trade in positive territory over the year to date, benefiting from the higher interest rate environment and banks’ solid profitability and strong capital positions. Euro area banks had continued to reduce their domestic exposures in total government bond holdings. This suggested that they were less exposed to domestic shocks, as portfolios had become more diversified.

Concerns about inflation, financial conditions and fiscal policy had also extended to broader equity markets, with euro area stocks underperforming. A further factor weighing on equity markets globally had been the sharp correction in tech stocks, as growing concerns about the increased debt financing of the AI build-out and the returns it would generate had caused significant volatility . The substantial increase in debt issuance by hyperscalers to finance AI investment had so far been smoothly absorbed in euro area corporate bond markets, but at a higher cost for issuers.

Weakening risk sentiment towards the euro area and diverging interest rates had been reflected in the EUR/USD exchange rate, which had depreciated noticeably since the September meeting. Overall, financial conditions had tightened recently, mainly owing to a correction in risk assets and higher sovereign yields, although partly offset by the weakening of the exchange rate.

Ms Schnabel then turned to short -term funding markets. Bank borrowing costs in overnight repo markets had continued their gradual upward trend , with the spreads between rates for French, Italian and Spanish collateral broadly stable against those using German collateral. Liquidity redistribution across banks had continued to operate smoothly, with money market conditions adjusting well to an environment with less excess liquidity. On 27 October 2026, recourse to the Eurosystem’s standard refinancing operations had risen to its highest level since the end of 2016 , with short-term money market rates remaining close to the deposit facility rate. Both the seven-day main refinancing operation, which covered the October 2026 month-end, and the three-month longer-term refinancing operation, which covered the 2026 year-end, had contributed to the increase. Overall, this was a comforting sign that banks were becoming more accustomed to using standard refinancing operations in their day-to-day liquidity management as balance sheet normalisation and the reduction of excess liquidity progressed.

Mr Lane then went through the latest economic, monetary and financial developments in the global economy and the euro area.

Starting with inflation in the euro area, Mr Lane noted that headline inflation, as measured by the Harmonised index of Consumer Prices (HICP), had risen to 3.8% in September, from 3.2% in August. This increase had been driven by energy price inflation, which had increased markedly to 18.9% from 14.3%. Diesel and petrol prices had reached new peaks in September, in part reflecting elevated refining margins. Inflation excluding energy had risen to 2.3% in September, from 2.1% in August. Food inflation had increased by 0.2 percentage points in September, to 1.3%, in part owing to the impact of the summer heatwaves on the unprocessed food component. Core inflation (HICP inflation excluding energy and food) had edged up to 2.5% in September, from 2.4% in August: a 0.1 percentage point decline in goods inflation to 1.1% had been offset by a 0.2 percentage point increase in services inflation to 3.2%.

The pass-through of the energy shock to inflation remained most visible in direct effects. Indirect effects had, overall, evolved as expected and were still limited. So far there had been no material signs of second-round effects. Indicators of underlying inflation had remained broadly stable and wage pressures remained moderate. Compensation per employee had grown by 3.3% in the second quarter, down from 3.6% in the first quarter, while rising productivity had helped contain the growth of unit labour costs. At the same time, the early stages of the pricing chain pointed to upward pressures. The ECB’s forward-looking wage tracker suggested that negotiated wage growth would fluctuate between 2.5% and 2.8% in the remaining months of 2026 and average 2.6% in the first three quarters of 2027 , broadly in line with the September staff projections. However, in the composite Purchasing Managers’ Index ( PMI ) input prices had picked up to 67.3 in October, from 67.0 in September and 62.8 in August. In addition, the selling price expectations of firms over the coming year had increased in the latest round of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises in the euro area. These signals suggested that indirect and second-round effects would become more material over time, as anticipated in the September staff projections.

Market and survey-based inflation expectations over shorter horizons had risen, but most measures of longer-term inflation expectations stood at around 2%, supporting the stabilisation of inflation around target in the medium term. Estimates of market-implied inflation expectations (derived from measures of inflation compensation by adjusting for risk premia) averaged 3.1% for 2026, 3.3% for 2027 and 2.1% for 2028 . Expectations of professional forecasters for headline inflation had been revised up for 2027 but were unrevised for 2028 at 2.0%. Medium to longer-term inflation expectations of consumers were broadly stable, as were expectations of firms, according to the second quarter and third quarter rounds of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises.

Brent crude oil prices (front month – based on futures ) had increased by 13% to USD 115 per barrel since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting, in an environment of heightened volatility , elevated freight rates and high global prices for refined products. Price pressures had been particularly pronounced for physical Brent contracts, which reflected prices for more immediate delivery than the front-month prices. Gas prices had increased by 22% to €97 per MWh over the same period, owing to upward pressure from the Middle East conflict. The euro had depreciated by 4.0% against the US dollar since the September meeting, and by 2.2% in nominal effective terms.

The incoming information pointed to continued global economic growth in the third quarter, with the global composite output PMI (excluding the euro area) increasing to 54.5 in September, reflecting expansion in both the manufacturing and services sectors. At the same time, stocks of finished goods had increased to well above their long -term averages, suggesting some hoarding of finished goods to insulate against persistent uncertainties. Global trade continued to grow , bolstered by AI-related demand, but had shifted from goods to services.

For the euro area, the incoming data suggested that the economy had continued to expand in the third quarter. The October figure of 51.9 for the composite output PMI remained in expansionary territory, although it was slightly lower than the readings for August (52.0) and September (53.1). Both the services and manufacturing PMIs signalled expansion. Manufacturing, digital services and exports were benefiting from AI-related business investment. Government spending on infrastructure and defence was also supporting activity. These factors should continue to underpin growth in the near term. At the same time, renewed energy price increases had hit consumer confidence and higher financing costs were likely to weigh on growth.

As regards the labour market, the unemployment rate had remained at 6.4% in August. Growth in employment and the labour force remained subdued, while productivity had gradually picked up. Indeed job postings had moved sideways in recent months, while the composite employment PMI remained just above the 50 threshold. The unemployment expectations of consumers for one year ahead had risen to the highest level since the start of the Middle East conflict, but expectations in the Survey of Professional Forecasters were little changed. While the survey pointed to a gradual moderation in the unemployment rate , to 6.3% in 2027 and 6.2% 2028, this was above the rates in the September staff projections, which saw unemployment at 6.1% in 2027 and 5.9% in 2028.

Turning to fiscal policies, the profile continued to be one of significant loosening in 2026 followed by a significant tightening in 2027 and 2028. Newly specified fiscal measures since the September staff projections reinforced that pattern , with some additional loosening this year and some additional tightening next year.

Over the medium term, a recovery in confidence and real incomes, driven by gradually declining energy prices and a robust labour market, should bolster domestic demand. Investment in AI-related activities and government spending on infrastructure and defence should also continue to support growth. Export growth should pick up on the back of strengthening foreign demand.

Financial conditions had tightened since the Governing Council’s previous monetary policy meeting. Interest rates had broadly moved up, while stock prices had fallen. The increase in interest rates had been part of a more general trend in global financial markets, reflecting the fallout from the Middle East conflict and high debt issuance in the public and private sectors in many economies. As the rise in long-term yields had been driven in part by higher real risk premia, it constituted a tightening impulse that would contribute to restraining demand.

The cost of market-based debt for firms had risen to 4.1% in August, from 4.0% in July, while bank lending rates for firms had remained at 3.8%. Growth in bank lending to firms had slowed to an annual rate of 4.2% in August and September, from 4.4% in July, while corporate bond issuance had grown at an annual rate of 4.2% in September, up from 3.8% in August and 3.5% in July. Credit standards for loans to firms had tightened in the third quarter, with banks citing concern about the economic risks faced by their customers. The latest round of the Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises corroborated the message of tightening credit conditions, as firms had widely reported a further net tightening in bank lending rates. Despite higher financing needs for inventories and working capital, demand for corporate loans had declined, reflecting in particular higher interest rates. Mortgage rates had risen to 3.6% in August, from 3.5% in July, while mortgage lending growth had edged down to 3.0% in September. Credit standards for mortgage lending had been unchanged in the third quarter, whereas demand for mortgages had declined substantially given higher interest rates.

Based on the assessment of the incoming information against the three elements of the Governing Council’s reaction function, Mr Lane proposed that the Governing Council keep the three key ECB interest rates unchanged. Energy prices had increased beyond the baseline path foreseen in the September ECB staff projections, posing upside risks to the inflation outlook and downside risks to the growth outlook. The increase was likely to raise inflation further in the near term and keep headline inflation well above target over the coming quarters. Thereafter, declining energy inflation, together with the effects of higher interest rates, should support the return of inflation to target. While the full effects of the energy shock were still unfolding, underlying inflation had remained broadly stable so far and wages did not show a material response at this stage. The interest rate hikes in June and September left the Governing Council well positioned to navigate the current elevated uncertainty. The December projections, which would extend the forecast horizon to include 2029, would provide an updated integrated assessment of how the energy shock, AI-related dynamics, the shift in financing conditions and all other relevant developments were shaping the inflation outlook and the surrounding risks. The data that had come in by December would also help the Governing Council to assess developments in underlying inflation and the strength of monetary transmission.

Regarding the economic analysis, members agreed with the assessment provided by Mr Lane in his introduction. Starting with the external environment, the global economy was continuing to prove more resilient than expected, notwithstanding further increases in energy prices, tighter financial conditions and elevated geopolitical tensions. The incoming information pointed to steady global economic growth in the third quarter, with the global composite output PMI (excluding the euro area) increasing in September, reflecting expansion in both the manufacturing and services sectors. Global activity was being supported by AI investment, inventory accumulation and the fact that tariffs had turned out to be lower than initially announced. AI was driving an investment boom, bolstering global trade and the manufacturing cycle. Inventory accumulation was in part related to some hoarding of finished goods to insulate against persistent uncertainties.

While it was noted that the resilience of economic growth had persisted despite the headwinds of higher energy prices, geopolitical uncertainties and tighter financial conditions, concern was expressed about how far AI investment growth and inventory accumulation could be relied on to continue providing support to global activity. The Middle East conflict and geopolitical tensions had persisted much longer than initially anticipated. Uncertainty, including about a potential intensification of geopolitical tensions, remained elevated. The positive impact of AI investment on global economic activity and its broader global inflation implications needed to be monitored. On the one hand, AI investment growth was supporting economic activity and global demand via manufacturing activity, investment and trade, and was thereby increasing inflation. On the other hand, if AI raised productivity, it could be disinflationary. Specifically, it could lower employment and curtail the ability of firms to raise prices.

Turning to commodity markets, members noted that energy prices had gone above the adverse scenario of the September projections. Not only had crude oil prices risen further, but increases in energy prices had also broadened and strengthened, including for natural gas and refined products, especially diesel. This development was linked to geopolitical tensions and supply-side factors. Euro area natural gas prices had tripled since the start of the conflict in the Middle East and were now at their highest level since 2022. As for liquid fuel prices, the initial shock seemed to have been absorbed to some degree by adjustments in both supply and demand. The renewed spike appeared to be due to an anticipation of further escalations in the Middle East conflict. On the one hand, there was little indication that the conflict in the Middle East would be resolved soon, suggesting an even more prolonged energy price shock. On the other hand, the geopolitical origins of the energy shock created two-sided risks as regards the direction of energy prices. The spread between the price of refined diesel and the price of crude oil had widened, owing in large part to supply disruptions in the Middle East and in Russia, as well as a reduction in supply from China. The current high levels of prices for refined products were seen as worrying, as they could feed into transport, shipping, agricultural and production costs, spreading the impact beyond that of the direct energy component of inflation. Food commodity prices, especially in Asia, were also coming under pressure owing to adverse weather conditions linked to the “El Nino” phenomenon. While it was noted that staff had already incorporated some lagged effects from energy price increases and weather conditions into their food inflation projections, further effects could materialise next year as new contracts and price agreements were established for food production. Energy prices could ease if the current premium for diesel spurred the use of the available capacity to narrow the global supply gap, or, if the geopolitical situation were to improve, the associated risk premium could unwind relatively quickly. Conversely, gas prices could rise further if supply were disrupted further or an unusually cold winter coincided with low storage levels, amid global competition for liquified natural gas.

With regard to domestic economic activity, members concurred with the assessment presented by Mr Lane. Despite higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions, euro area economic growth had continued to display some resilience and had performed better than expected so far. The incoming data suggested that the euro area economy had continued to expand in the third quarter of the year. Services had recovered, after weakening at the start of the Middle East conflict. Manufacturing, digital services and exports were benefiting from AI-related business investment. Government spending on infrastructure and defence was also supporting activity. These factors should continue to underpin growth in the near term. At the same time, renewed energy price increases had hit consumer confidence, and higher financing costs were likely to weigh on growth.

Despite higher energy prices and tighter financial conditions, the October PMI still signalled expansion in the manufacturing and services sectors. There was some indication of positive, albeit not strong, growth momentum in some sectors, particularly those linked to AI and to defence and infrastructure spending in Germany. The euro area had benefited from AI-related activity in the first two quarters of the year, with the services most involved in the digitalisation process accounting for about one-third of growth in value added, which was a good sign for the future.

While growth had held up at around 0.2-0.3% per quarter, there were some signs that economic activity might be slowing, particularly as the PMI had declined markedly in October and consumer confidence and private consumption had weakened. The short-term growth outlook was considered to be gloomier than previously expected and downside signals were more visible, although it was noted that near-term growth expectations reported in the Survey of Monetary Analysts had been revised up.

Looking ahead, members generally agreed that tightening financial conditions and the renewed spike in energy prices would have a negative effect on growth, although its magnitude remained to be seen. The decline in demand for loans suggested a stronger adverse effect on activity than had been seen so far, although some of the effect from higher rates on private investment spending, housing and consumption might be attenuated by the weaker exchange rate. The more recent surge in energy prices since August was creating a stronger headwind and, overall, higher energy prices still had to feed through to euro area activity and become visible in GDP data.

Private consumption, having previously developed in line with the projected recovery, had begun to weaken. There were a number of factors at play. Higher energy prices were having an impact on real incomes and were weakening consumer confidence. Higher interest rates had increased incentives to save and to reduce consumption. The sharp decline in demand for housing loans and rising mortgage rates could start to weigh on housing investment. One area of support was strong demand for tourism services. Over the medium term, recovering confidence and real incomes, supported by gradually declining energy prices and a robust labour market, were expected to strengthen domestic demand.

Business investment was being supported by AI-related activity, but there were increasingly questions as to how long this factor (alongside lower than initially announced tariffs) might continue to provide support. Higher borrowing costs and tighter credit standards were expected to constrain investment more broadly.

The euro area labour market had remained largely resilient, although there were some signs of softening. The unemployment rate had remained near historical lows in August. Employment and the labour force continued to grow, albeit at a subdued pace, while productivity had gradually picked up. Job postings had remained stable in recent months and the composite employment PMI remained just above the threshold of 50. The unemployment rate expectations of professional forecasters as reported in the Survey of Professional Forecasters were little changed and continued to point to a gradual decline in the unemployment rate from the current level. However, consumers’ expectations for unemployment one year ahead had risen to the highest level seen since the start of the Middle East conflict. An additional factor to consider was the potential impact of AI on productivity and jobs.

The fiscal stance, while providing support to growth in 2026 through defence and infrastructure spending, was likely to be tighter in 2027. At the same time, upcoming elections could result in more spending than currently envisaged. By contrast, elevated fiscal and political uncertainty could weigh on growth.

Members considered that, over the medium term, a recovery in confidence and real incomes, driven by gradually declining energy prices and a robust labour market, should bolster domestic demand. Investment in AI-related activities and government spending on infrastructure and defence should also continue to support growth. Export growth should pick up on the back of strengthening foreign demand.

Concerning structural and fiscal policies, members reiterated that higher potential growth required structural reform and had to be underpinned by sound public finances. Fiscal sustainability was a crucial anchor for broader economic stability. Governments needed to be proactive in enhancing fiscal sustainability. To this end, fiscal responses to the energy shock should be temporary, targeted and tailored.

Increasing the euro area’s growth potential required structural reform: simplifying and harmonising rules across the EU’s Single Market, accelerating the energy transition and completing the savings and investments union. These were key building blocks for making the euro area economy more dynamic and resilient. As the process for agreeing on the legal framework for the digital euro moved into its final stage, members reiterated the importance of reaching agreement on the European Commission’s Single Currency Package as quickly as possible.

Against this background, members assessed that the risks to the growth outlook were to the downside. This was due, in particular, to the Middle East conflict and recent developments in Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine. Continued disruption of energy supplies could cause energy prices to rise further and for longer than currently expected. This would weigh on real incomes, spending and investment. A worsening of global financial market sentiment or intensifying spillovers in global bond markets could tighten financing conditions and thereby dampen demand. Fiscal uncertainty might also further tighten financing conditions and weaken confidence, thereby lowering consumption and investment. A resurgence of trade tensions between major economies could further disrupt supply chains, reduce exports and weaken consumption and investment. By contrast, growth could turn out to be higher if the economy and energy markets were to adapt more quickly than expected to the disruption caused by the ongoing conflicts or if these were resolved sustainably. Moreover, the adoption of new technologies by euro area firms and government spending on infrastructure and defence, as well as reforms to enhance productivity and complete the EU’s Single Market, might drive up growth by more than expected.

With regard to price developments, members concurred with the assessment presented by Mr Lane in his introduction, noting that, on the one hand, energy prices had increased beyond the baseline path foreseen in the September ECB staff projections, which was likely to raise inflation further in the near term and keep headline inflation well above target over the coming year. On the other hand, underlying inflation had remained broadly stable in recent months and wage growth data had moderated further.

Energy price inflation had increased markedly, to 18.9%, from 14.3% in August. Other components of consumer price inflation, however, including food, non-energy goods and services, were either in line with or slightly lower than what had been previously expected. news.summary:
Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.

Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.

See the most recent developments below.

Gen. Sardar Shekarchi, spokesperson of Iran's armed forces, denies that Iran carried out a drone attack on Kuwait. According to Iran's official state news agency IRNA, Shekarchi "categorically and completely" rejected claims by the Kuwaiti military that Iranian forces attacked vital Kuwaiti sites. "No military or offensive operations have been conducted by the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the region," Shekarchi said, according to IRNA. "Given the history of hostile actions -- including the use of 'false flag' tactics and regional adventurism by the Zionist regime and U.S. forces -- these accusations should be viewed as a cover for continued malevolence and an attempt to exacerbate insecurity in the region," Shekarchi said. Kuwaiti authorities have blamed Iran for the attack that killed two Italian nationals and injured one Kuwaiti and one Pakistani national. -ABC News' Jamie Dorrington

The two Italian nationals injured in Thursday's Iranian drone attack in Kuwait have died, a spokesperson for Kuwait's Ministry of Defense said in a statement. Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her condolences to the victim's families in a post on X. "On behalf of myself and the Government, I express my deepest sorrow and extend my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families. My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families," Meloni said. -ABC News' Othon Leyva

The Kuwait Army on Thursday reported that four people were injured by falling shrapnel after an Iranian drone attack targeted "a vital site" in the Gulf state. The army said in a post to X that Kuwaiti forces "dealt with" the incoming drones. "Material damage also occurred," the statement added. Those injured were two Italian nationals, one Pakistani national and one Kuwaiti national, the army said.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps on Thursday claimed that two oil tankers transiting the Strait of Hormuz without permission from Tehran "were hit by sea mines" north of the Omani port of Khasab. The IRGC statement was published by the semi-official Fars News Agency.

Renewed fighting in Yemen's civil war has forced more than 364,000 people from their homes since August, including tens of thousands over the past week, the United Nations' humanitarian chief said in a statement Wednesday after he arrived in the port city of Aden in the south of the country. "Fighting, insecurity and heavy restrictions along key supply routes are preventing families from accessing the food and medicine they need to survive," UN Under Secretary General for Humanitarian Affairs Tom Fletcher said, noting that half of Yemen's population needs aid. "Millions are hungry," he added. Fletcher also called on the Houthi rebels to "immediately and unconditionally release our detained UN colleagues and other humanitarians." "Our work and our people must be protected," he said. Since 2014, Yemen's internationally-recognized, Saudi-backed government -- now based in Aden -- has been fighting with the Iran-backed Houthis, which occupy the capital Sana'a. The conflict has become a widening front in the regional war involving Iran that began in February.

Mohammed Huwais/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: A Yemeni boy inspects the damage following a strike allegedly carried out by Saudi forces that targeted a horse farm on the outskirts of Sanaa on Nov. 24, 2026.

-ABC News' Morgan Winsor

A military spokesperson for the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen said on Wednesday that the group launched new strikes targeting the financial district in Riyadh and a key Saudi oil refinery. In a video statement, Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said the operation against the financial district in Riyadh "caused extensive damage." The Ras Tanura refinery in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province was also targeted, causing "fires to break out there," Saree said. Early on Wednesday morning, a Saudi military spokesman said four drones had been intercepted in Ras Tanura and "a number of fragments fell as a result of the interception, with no casualties." Satellite images showed black smoke above the Ras Tanura oil refinery on Wednesday.

Nasa Worldview/via Reuters - PHOTO: A satellite image shows a large smoke cloud billowing over Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery on Nov. 25, 2026.

-ABC News' Nasser Atta and Othon Leyva

President Donald Trump said the ongoing war with Iran is "funded" through January, when Democrats take control of Congress and could reign in his authority to authorize the conflict. In an interview with the New York Post conducted in the Oval Office on Tuesday afternoon, Trump said the incoming Democratic majority will "take a total win and make it a loss." Trump again touted the U.S. military success against Iran. "Their navy's gone, their air force is gone, their anti-aircraft, everything's gone. Their leaders are gone. I mean, if [Democrats] do that, they'll just take a win and make it a loss," Trump said. When pressed on whether his timeframe to freely launch renewed strikes is narrowing, Trump reportedly said he finds it "hard to believe" that Democrats would stop the war. "I don't know how they could do that politically, because we have a win. We can put that war to bed anytime we want," Trump said, according to the Post. Israel's goal of ending the Islamic Republic is "probably doable," Trump also said, but told the Post that regime change is not his goal. "I just don't want them to have a nuclear weapon. I was never for or against regime change, that was never a criteria for me," Trump said. Trump also addressed an Iranian announcement this week that it would be suing the U.S. for compensation for an airstrike on a school. "Well, I want compensation for the people that they've killed, which is far more because they've killed, first of all, they killed 75,000 protesters in the last seven months. But they've killed our people for years," Trump replied, according to the Post. "The USS Cole, they've killed many, many hundreds of Americans. So if they want to play the compensation game, we win," the president said. -ABC News' Isabella Murray

The U.S. is investigating whether Iran is behind a series of cyberattacks that targeted energy tankers, according to multiple officials. At least 50 ships are believed to have been attacked, with some receiving bomb threats that purported to say the ship was to be detonated. The U.S. has identified Iran as the prime suspect, but are also investigating whether Russia could also be the suspect. The threats are believed to scare boats into not traversing overseas. The Coast Guard has helped thwart all of the cyber attacks, according to officials. They've also posted a warning on their website telling tankers to patch their systems, prior to a cyber event occurring. "Just as we monitor for mechanical or weather-related hazards, we incorporate cyber risk management into our routine, professional approach to facilitating commerce and ensuring safe vessel transits into and from our ports and waterway," according to a Coast Guard spokesperson. Earlier this year, two boats headed to Texas were boarded by U.S. Coast Guard teams after it was discovered that cyber incidents occurred onboard.

A tower in the financial district of the Saudi capital Riyadh was targeted in a "terrorist attack," a Saudi military spokesman said Tuesday. "One of the towers of the financial center was targeted in a cowardly terrorist attack," Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, the spokesman for Saudi-led coalition forces fighting the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen, posted on X. The post did not provide details about the nature of the attack. One of the towers in the Riyadh financial center was damaged last week when it was hit by a projectile. -ABC News' Othon Leyva

The United Kingdom Maritime Operations (UKMTO) Centre on Tuesday issued a warning after it received a report of three vessels being struck by projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday evening. The vessels were reported to have continued their transit with all crew members accounted for, UKMTO said. Separately, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy on Tuesday claimed that several tankers hit naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, the Islamic Republic News Agency reported. The IRGC Navy said the vessels were traveling through the strait "illegally." The IRGC has repeatedly claimed vessels have been damaged by naval mines, but U.S. Central Command has called previous claims false. -ABC News' Othon Leyva

news.summary: The number of tankers carrying energy products through the Strait of Hormuz has increased in November despite the fact that the number of attacks and incidents with mines has hit the highest level since the beginning of the Iran war. Between November 1 and 19, the seven-day moving average count showed more than 26 crude oil, fuel, and LNG tankers transiting the Strait each day, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing ship-tracking data by Vortexa. To compare, the seven-day moving average was below 25 vessels on at least two-thirds of the days in October. The vessel numbers come with two caveats. First, the above-mentioned numbers may not be all tankers that have transited or attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz, due to signal interference and en masse switching off of the transponders on the ships. The other is that there has been a slight reduction in the number of very large crude carriers VLCCs and Suezmaxes moving through the chokepoint, but the number of smaller tankers, Aframaxes, has increased, according to Vortexa’s data. The change in the tanker fleet operating in and out of the Strait of Hormuz makes it even more difficult for analysts to estimate how much crude oil and fuel are being evacuated from the Persian Gulf and exit the Strait en route to international markets. Smaller oil tankers moved in October the most volumes of crude oil out of the Strait of Hormuz since the war began, as Iran targets supertankers and incidents with naval mines and unknown projectiles hit a wartime high. Moreover, a record number of the so-called long-range-2 LR2 clean tankers that have transported fuels such as diesel and gasoline have become the so-called dirty tankers and started shipping crude. The LR2 tankers are similar in capacity to the Aframax crude tankers, which can ship up to 800,000 barrels of crude each. A clean-turned-dirty LR2 tanker could be employed on the complex trade shuffles near the Strait of Hormuz, where shuttle-shipments have become the prevailing mode of moving crude oil out of the Persian Gulf in recent months. The EU also stressed that the OPEC cartel has a responsibility to maintain balance in the oil market, the official said.

news.summary: Africa’s largest refinery will soon become the biggest public firm with a primary listing on the continent, too, after the $1.6-billion initial public offering valued Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals at $48 billion. The Dangote refinery of Africa’s richest man, Aliko Dangote, is set to overtake Johannesburg-listed Capitec Ltd and Gold Fields Ltd, each with a market cap of about $30 billion, when it debuts on the stock exchange in Lagos next month, according to Bloomberg’s calculations. The initial public offering IPO of a minority stake in Dangote Petroleum Refinery in Nigeria closed at the end of last month, with investors from 120 countries, including all 54 African countries, applying to buy shares. Applications are currently being checked, and the next step is the SEC reviewing how shares are allocated.    The listing in Lagos is provisionally expected for December 1. The IPO could raise as much as $2.1 billion if the company exercises its greenshoe option, which is now almost a given, considering the record-high interest in the float. Proceeds are expected to be invested in a $14-billion plan to double the Dangote refinery’s crude processing capacity from nearly 700,000 barrels per day bpd now to 1.4 million bpd by 2029.  The IPO of the Dangote refinery is Africa’s biggest and will greatly expand the number of retail investors in Nigeria and the continent. The Dangote refinery is going public as Aliko Dangote is targeting 10 million retail investors in the “IPO for the people” pitch. “With a minimum subscription of just 10 shares, the offer is designed to give ordinary Nigerians and Africans an opportunity to own a stake in the refinery,” Aliko Dangote said at the IPO launch in early September. “The IPO is positioned not simply as a capital-raising exercise, but as an opportunity for workers, entrepreneurs and everyday Nigerians to participate in the refinery’s future growth,” according to Dangote. news.title: Faisal Islam: Why Trump's new tariffs are less of a threat - BBC
news.summary:
There was none of last April's fanfare, the Rose Garden reveal, the gameshow blue board or "Liberation Day" rhetoric surrounding Trump's tariff announcement this week.

Instead there is something rather tentative about this latest exercise with talk of further negotiations.

"We expect to have a broad, even a plurilateral negotiation to talk about excess capacity and how to resolve it," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC.

Around the world the view is that this week's announcement is an attempt to shore up the domestic legal underpinning of these tariffs, more than a fundamental change in the Trump trade agenda.

The tariffs are also not due to come in until January or possibly February, after a period of consultation. There has already been eight months of process and hearings, and the rates announced are upper ceilings, often up for negotiation. It's quite the contrast to the overnight shock meted out to the world last April.

Still, the USA is making the argument that large swathes of the rest of the world, including allies, are harming the US goods trade position by supporting their own industries. This is the basis for the tariffs, in large part replacing the previous tariffs justified on "forced labour" provisions.

The UK, which was unaffected by the new tariff announcements, remains caught by the forced labour provisions, albeit at a rate of 10% extra on global tariffs. There was no move in response to the UK's digital services tax.

It means for many important countries there are now two legal bases upon which the Trump tariffs rest, after the Supreme Court struck down the original emergency basis earlier this year. A group of 25 states has taken the Trump administration to court to strike down the forced labour tariffs.

The tariffs will have to be finalised under a Democrat Congress, which has influence, but not power. The Speaker-designate Hakeem Jeffries said this week that the new House would in its first 100 days "move aggressively to… repeal the Trump tariffs".

The Chinese rate of 20% is the truce rate from last year's Trump-Xi deal. The truce is due to expire in mid-January. Beijing's response was muted, no retaliation, criticism of industrial overcapacity as a "false issue", and a call to implement the Xi-Trump deal. The leverage over China has weakened, with the US share of its exports dropping to around 10% this year, down from 15%, just two years ago, and 19% in 2018.

However, the most interesting spot to focus on is closer to home for Trump. Over half of Canada tariffs are authorised under "Section 338" of the 1930s Smoot-Hawley act. There is already a Senate Bill to repeal them, and it is possible that there would be enough rebel Republicans in the House and Senate to threaten to over-ride any Presidential veto. The incoming Senate Finance Committee chair Ron Wyden last week said Democrats were focussed on "figuring out a way to beat Trump and his veto".

Before that an interim deal is being sought, and Democrat senators such as Chris Coons are appearing on Canadian TV, telling CBC : "Frankly, if you can get an interim deal, I'd take it, and then put it to us in the new majority to legislate an even better deal."

The rest of world is watching the machinations in Washington and also looking beyond Donald Trump's tenure.

It pays to look at how the initial Trump trade-quake has reshaped the pattern of world trade already.

The rest of the world has rerouted its trade flows around Donald Trump's tariff wall, proving far more resilient than expected. In cash terms, China's exports so far in 2026 are down about 8% on 2024, but that is more than 25 times made up for by its increased exports to everywhere else.

Canada has seen flat exports to the USA since tariffs, fewer cars and lumber, but pricier flows of energy. Its exports, especially commodities, to the rest of the world have rocketed.

This means that next month's G20 summit at the president's Miami resort is an important moment. In general US allies have not rocked the boat, accepting the lower level of tariffs as part of the new reality. Could the middle powers choose to upset their host in Florida next month?

The bigger question however, is how much the Democrats decide to keep of the America First trade agenda. It will not be all, but nor will it be nothing. Economists now expect some of these tariffs to stay in place for years.
